'''Władysław J. (Wladek) Świątecki''' (22 April 1926 – 30 September 2009) was a Polish theoretical and nuclear physicist. He was one of the first proponents of the [[island of stability]] for [[superheavy element]]s, showing that it appears in a mass formula influenced by the presence of [[nuclear shell model|closed nuclear shells]]; he is also known for several other contributions in [[nuclear structure]] research.

==Biography==
Świątecki was born in Paris on 22 April 1926. His father, also named [[Władysław Świątecki (inventor)|Władysław Świątecki]], was an inventor and [[aeronautical engineer]]. Świątecki lived in [[Poland]] with his family until September 1939, when they escaped to France following the [[invasion of Poland]] and start of [[World War II]], only to flee again to England in May 1940.<ref name=obituary/>

Świątecki continued his education in England. In 1945 and 1946 respectively, Świątecki completed [[Bachelor's degree]]s in physics and mathematics. In 1950, under the guidance of Rudolf Peierls, he received his [[Ph.D.]] in physics for his thesis entitled "The Surface Energy of Nuclei".<ref name=obituary/>

Having completed his education, Świątecki went on to work in various nuclear physics laboratories in Scandinavia before settling at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] in 1957. He worked at the [[Niels Bohr Institute]] in [[Copenhagen]] for three years, then spent another three in [[Uppsala]] at the [[Gustav Werner Institute]], and finally one year at the [[University of Aarhus]]. At Berkeley, Świątecki did extensive work in [[nuclear physics]], and continued to do so even after his formal retirement in 1991.<ref name=obituary/>

Świątecki died peacefully in his home on 30 September 2009 from [[pancreatic cancer]]. He has 5 children and 8 grandchildren.<ref name=legacy>{{cite web |url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/sfgate/obituary.aspx?n=wladyslaw-j-swiatecki&pid=135263647 |title=Wladyslaw J. Swiatecki |publisher=Legacy.com |date=1 November 2009 |access-date=20 July 2019}}</ref>

==Research==
Świątecki was a pioneer in several areas of nuclear physics, including studies of [[nuclear fission]] of superheavy elements, the [[nuclear shell model]], and the development of a [[semi-empirical mass formula]].<ref name=obituary/> Although the original formulation of the nuclear shell model predates Świątecki, he and [[Gertrude Scharff-Goldhaber]] from [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] calculated that "[[magic number (physics)|magic numbers]]" of [[proton]]s and [[neutron]]s may exist for some superheavy elements and confer additional stability, whose estimated [[half-lives]] ranged from minutes to millions of years.<ref name=lblnews>{{cite news |title=Superheavy Element 114 Confirmed: A Stepping Stone to the Island of Stability |date=24 September 2009 |publisher=Berkeley Lab |access-date=20 July 2019 |url=https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2009/09/24/114-confirmed/}}</ref> In 1966, Świątecki, along with William Myers and Heiner Meldner, developed a model that revealed an increase in [[fission barrier]] height for nuclei centered around [[atomic number]] [[flerovium|114]], suggesting the possibility of stabilizing shell effects in that region. Although several other such regions were proposed, including one around [[element 126]] as early as 1957, Świątecki and Myers determined that the [[Coulomb force]] would shift the proton shell closure to ''Z'' = 114. With this work, the theory of an "island of stability" for superheavy [[nuclide]]s gained popularity, and motivated experiments seeking such nuclides in subsequent decades.<ref name=quest>{{cite journal |last1=Bemis |first1=C. E. |last2=Nix |first2=J. R. |date=1977 |title=Superheavy elements - the quest in perspective |journal=Comments on Nuclear and Particle Physics |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=65–78 |url=http://inspirehep.net/record/1382449/files/v7-n3-p65.pdf|issn=0010-2709}}</ref>

In addition to his prediction of the island of stability, Świątecki's contributions led to further developments in the nuclear shell model, most notably the macroscopic-microscopic method for calculating various properties of nuclei and extrapolating to unknown nuclei.<ref name=obituary/> The 1994 [[Thomas-Fermi model]] of Myers and Świątecki offered several new developments, namely a solution to an anomaly in nuclear curvature.<ref name=macromicro>{{cite conference |last1=Nix |first1=J. R. |last2=Möller |first2=P. |title=Macroscopic-microscopic mass models |date=1995 |conference=International Conference on Exotic Nuclei and Atomic Masses |location=Arles, France |id=LA-UR-95-2073 |arxiv=nucl-th/9507015}}</ref>

Świątecki also did some research in [[chaos theory]] and its implications for nuclear dynamics.<ref name=chaos>{{cite journal |last1=Blocki |first1=J. |last2=Shi |first2=J. J. |last3=Świątecki |first3=W. J. |title=Order, chaos, and nuclear dynamics |date=1993 |journal=Nuclear Physics A |volume=554 |issue=3 |pages=387–412 |doi=10.1016/0375-9474(93)90227-O |bibcode=1993NuPhA.554..387B |url=https://escholarship.org/content/qt0923379t/qt0923379t.pdf?t=p0hhfy}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
In 1973, Świątecki became a member of the [[Royal Danish Academy of Sciences and Letters]].<ref name=obituary/> He was also a member of the [[Polish Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. In recognition for his work, he won the 1990 [[Marian Smoluchowski Medal]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://old.ptf.net.pl/ptf3.html |title=Laureates of the Marian Smoluchowski Medal |publisher=Polish Physical Society |access-date=21 July 2019}}</ref> of the [[Polish Physical Society]] (for which he was a laureate in 1989), and received an honorary degree from the [[Jagiellonian University]] in [[Kraków]] in 2000.<ref name=berk1/>
